## Known order-dependent failures

The working list lives on the `chore/random_order_audit` branch, as [`internal/order_dependent_specs.md`](https://github.com/fastlane/fastlane/blob/chore/random_order_audit/internal/order_dependent_specs.md). The same file is the input to `rake test_order_dependent`, so the table and the list of spec paths cannot drift apart.

That branch carries a workflow scoped to its own name, so it never runs on master, and it runs two jobs rather than the full matrix. It is expected to be red.

### Where it stands

All measured on CI at the pinned seed 48174, so the numbers are comparable run to run.

| | failures |
| --- | --- |
| baseline | 48 |
| after rows A, B, C, D, H, I, E, J | **5** |

The five left are one example each, and are the last row in the table: `supply/uploader_spec`, `spaceship/two_step_or_factor_client_spec`, `fastlane_core/device_manager_spec`, `fastlane/actions_specs/notification_spec`, `fastlane/actions_specs/automatic_code_signing_spec`.

### What the fixed rows were

Almost all of them were a per-example concern implemented as process wide state, and each one was a different global:

- **A.** The SIRP stub lived in the `common spaceship login` shared example, so a spec reaching a login without it computed a real SRP value that matched none of the recorded request bodies.
- **B.** `Spaceship::ConnectAPI` forwards to whatever `ConnectAPI.client` returns, and each client extends the API modules onto itself. A `@client` set by an earlier example won outright, and absent that an implicit client only wired up `provisioning_request_client` when a cookie, token or portal client was present.
- **C.** `Frameit.config` was set by one example group and read by others.
- **H and I.** `Spaceship::Base` subclasses each hold their own `@client`, stamped on by `set_client` and preferred over `Spaceship::Portal.client`. Class level ivars are not inherited, so clearing it on `PortalBase` does nothing for `Spaceship::Certificate`.
- **E and J.** Three separate causes in one file: mocking `Process.wait`, which is what fills in `$?` that `FastlanePty` reads for the exit status; a one shot "Logging disabled while running tests" banner absorbed by whichever example ran first; and `pty` being required lazily, so examples referencing the `PTY` constant depended on something else having run a pty backed command.

**D** is the exception and is pinned rather than fixed. `import_from_git_spec` is one scenario written as several examples: a `before :all` builds a git repository and individual examples append commits, tags and branches that later ones assert on. It is marked `order: :defined`, which makes the dependency explicit instead of accidental. It will need revisiting if the suite is ever split across processes, since the group has to stay whole and in order.

### Two things worth knowing

Fixing a row can reveal the next one. H was recorded as a suspected regression from the A fix and turned out not to be: the leak predated it and was masked because `spaceship_spec.rb` used to fail early and never reached the code that stamps the client. Expect the count to move up as well as down.

The second job runs only the affected files with a fresh seed each time, which samples orderings the full run never produces. It is a sampler and not a gate. On the latest run it found one of the five remaining failures rather than all five, because in a seventeen file context the other four do not have their triggering predecessors present.

### Also found, and parked

`FastlanePty.spawn_with_pty` reaps the child and then reads the exit status from `$?`, so the status crosses out of the `ensure` block as a thread global. `$?` is only written when the wait actually happens, so a command reports the status of whatever the thread ran last when the child was already reaped or a caller stubbed the wait. That is a user facing defect rather than an ordering one, and it is not part of this issue. Notes and a candidate patch are in `internal/notes/` on the branch, along with alternative approaches, since `wait2` is not obviously the best of them.

## Where this stands

The work is a stack of pull requests. Each is based on the one above it, so they are best reviewed top down and merged bottom up; each shrinks to its own commits as its parent lands.

| PR | Based on | What it fixes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #30190 ✅ | master | Module level configuration leaking between examples, plus the singleton guard that closes the class rather than the instances |
| #30192 | master | Spaceship client singletons, the `itc_service_key` cache and the session cookie store |
| #30193 | #30192 | Nine specs that each depended on something another example had done. No shared cause, which is why they are one pull request rather than five |
| #30194 | #30193 | The `ENV` guard: reports every variable that escapes the example that set it, independently of the order the suite ran in |
| #30195 | #30194 | State that outlives the process, in `/tmp` and in `HOME`, plus `rake test_isolated` |
| #30197 | #30195 | spaceship writing to a literal `/tmp`, in two places |
| #30200 | #30197 | A lazily required `PTY` constant, and SwiftLint crashing in its own error handler |
| #30201 | #30200 | The pty exit status travelling through `$?`. Fixes #30188 |
| #30191 🚧 | #30201 | Runs the suite as several processes, on macOS, Linux and Windows. The monitor for the work above |
| #30202 🚧 | #30191 | Makes the split the CI gate rather than a side workflow. Addresses #30189 |

All green as of now, including all three split platforms.

## Where the suite got to

7868 examples, 0 failures at random seeds, run serially, under an isolated `HOME`, and split across workers on all three platforms.

Locally the split runs in 88s against about 280s in one process. On the runners, macOS goes from 472-701s to 221s and Linux from 174s to 66s.

## The last three were found by splitting, not by seeds

Worth recording, because it is the argument for #30191 existing at all. A worker sees a subset of the suite that no random order produces, so a spec that depended on another file having run first fails there and nowhere else.

Adding Windows to the split found all three of these, and each turned out to be a product defect rather than a test one:

- **#30197**: spaceship logged to a literal `/tmp`, which on Windows resolves against the current drive and does not exist. It only ever worked because `fast_file_spec.rb` calls `FileUtils.mkdir_p('/tmp/fastlane/')` and sorts earlier in defined order. Every spaceship spec on Windows was relying on a spec in another tool to create a directory for it.
- **#30200**: SwiftLint reads `$?.exitstatus` in a `rescue`, which is nil when nothing in the process has run a subprocess. Unix never reaches that branch because `spec_helper` itself runs `which xar` as it loads. The suite was structurally unable to test it.
- **#30201**: the pty exit status crossed a block boundary through `$?`. The issue said this fixed no failing example; it now has two regression tests, each checked by reverting the fix first.

## Issues

| | |
| --- | --- |
| #30186 | `security cms -D` imports certificates into the user's default keychain when parsing provisioning profiles |
| #30187 | The suite writes to the developer's `HOME` and never cleans up |
| #30188 | `FastlanePty.spawn_with_pty` can report a previous command's exit status. Fixed by #30201 |
| #30189 | The suite is slow. Addressed by #30191 and #30202 |
| #30198 | `itc_service_key` reports local file errors as an App Store Connect outage, which is what made #30197 expensive to diagnose |

## Still to do

Recording the per platform timings on the runners and committing them, so the split is balanced by measured durations rather than by file size. A notes pull request with the methods and the measurements behind all of this. Retargeting each pull request to master as its parent merges.

## One thing reviewers should know

#30186 can redden the stack at random. `match/spec/runner_spec.rb` reaches for the real keychain and fails with "Could not install WWDR certificate" on some runners. It hit two of these PRs and both went green on rerun with identical code. If you see that failure, it is not the pull request.
